Only the listener's report loosens a limit, never time passing, and "mostly" means not yet. Loosen one step at a time: off limits to delicate, delicate to clear. Worse or stiffer the next morning means the last session was too much, and the limit tightens. A clinician's rule that allows one of the catalog's rehab drills the limit leaves out (the ankle circles and alphabet, the band ankle drills, towel scrunch, single-leg balance) goes into the row's rehab, with the listener's say-so; any other movement a clinician allows, such as a physio's slow calf raises, stays with the physio's plan.
- knee delicate left: clear once a full squat and going down stairs are pain-free, with nothing worse the next morning
Red flags, for the check-in, in chat (they stop the session before it starts, and suggest a clinician soon; the audio carries the opening's stop rule and heart rule instead): can't bear weight; rapidly increasing swelling; numbness or tingling; a joint that gives way or locks; pain that keeps getting worse after a week or two; dizziness that doesn't settle with rest; breathlessness that's suddenly getting worse; throbbing pain or swelling in one calf or thigh, with red, darkened or warm skin.
Emergencies, for the check-in, in chat (stop, and call emergency services now): chest pain, pressure or tightness, maybe spreading to the arm, neck or jaw; fainting or nearly fainting during exercise; a racing or irregular heartbeat with chest pain, breathlessness or feeling faint; leg pain or swelling with breathlessness or chest pain.

oser to failure than with a heavy weight. Don't promise one-rep strength from light kit; promise muscle and working strength.
- Load range: a timed set runs forty to sixty seconds at a steady pace, with a load that leaves two or three reps in reserve at the end. The effort rule holds as for counted sets. Timed sets suit steady whole-body work, where the coach talks with the listener through the set; heavy sets near the top of the load range stay counted.
- Rest and pairing: pair opposing muscles (push with pull) or upper with lower, so one rests while the other works, and give about a minute between the two halves of a pair. Unpaired sets get one to two minutes.
- Exercise order: put the multi-joint movements (squat, hinge, press, row) first, while fresh, unless the session's priority is a single-joint movement such as a rehab exercise, which then goes first. For muscle size alone, order is free.
- Tempo: keep each rep between about two and eight seconds in total (a three-second lowering is fine); never cue a single rep longer than about eight seconds. A slower lowering is a way to make a light weight harder, not a goal in itself.
- The order of steps when load is capped is house policy: a few more reps, a slower lowering, a pause at the hard point, more range, one arm or one leg, and only then the next dumbbell. Change one variable at a time.
- Progression: "too easy" moves the next session one step along that list; "too hard" moves one step back, or trims a set. Say in the audio what changed.
- Readiness and adjusting on the day: the check-in's readiness changes the plan. Normal: plan as usual, from the last loads. Low (tired, short on sleep, stressed): keep the length and the kind of work, drop about a third of the hard sets (a round, or a set per movement), hold last time's loads, end every set with three or four reps left, and leave out all-out efforts and the finisher; give the time to longer rests and easy mobility, and say why in the opening. Fresh, last one felt easy: one step along the progression order. Last one too hard: one step back, or a set fewer. Soreness from training keeps that muscle group light and well short of failure today; pain in a joint is a delicate limit for today. During the session, each main movement's first working set gets a target (reps and reps left) and ends with a self-check that offers one harder and one easier option for the sets after it, from the movement's notes and the progression order; on low readiness, offer only the easier option or holding steady. Never offer a harder option that loads a limited area more.
- Warm-up, finisher and cool-down: keep the warm-up short and specific: easy movement, then a lighter first set of the main movements, as a rehearsal and a check that the movement feels right today (not a promise of more reps). Close with slow breathing because it calms and ends the session well, and never claim it prevents soreness or injury. The finisher is a short, simple burst (house policy, not a study) and stays inside the injury rules.
- One-sided training: train both sides by default. When an injury rules out one side, training the healthy side still helps the injured one a little; say so in the audio, and never present it as a replacement for the injured side's own rehab.

## Equipment notes
**Hotel room (no gym).** Typically bodyweight, a chair, a bed edge, a towel, maybe a band. No mat: floor work goes on the carpet or a folded towel under the knees. A chair for support goes against a wall so it can't slide, and nothing pushes on a chair with wheels; the bed edge is fine for sitting and incline push-ups, too soft for step-ups. Towel rows go around a door handle only if the door is solid and closed toward the listener; when the door can't be trusted, the prone lat pulldown or the prone Y T W raise still gives the session its pull. Towel slides need a hard floor. Keep noise low; no jumping in hotel rooms.

**No equipment.** Bodyweight and some floor space. Everything still works: legs, glutes, core and pushing, with a chair or a wall to make it easier or harder. When standing is ruled out (an off-limits ankle or foot), seated conditioning (seated shadow boxing, arm pumps, speed bag) is what fills intervals and finishers; the brief's menu offers it once the limit removes the standing moves.

## Writing it
- First line of the draft: `movements: <every movement the script uses, by its name above, comma separated>`. Then the `@@ <seconds> | <label>` segments, adding up to exactly 900 s. You choose the segments: one can be a set, a pair, a whole round or the whole warm-up.
- Coach each movement from its notes (`movements --about`) (setup, cues, what one rep is, where to feel it, the faults and their fixes): fully the first time it appears, then a short reminder, so the rests and the easy work have room for the listener's world. Safety is the one hard rule (knowledge/script.md); beyond it, get the workout done and keep them engaged. What a voice can read: knowledge/tts-rules.md.
- Talk to time: Coach Freya speaks about 166 words a minute (estimated; not measured on this computer yet), so twenty seconds of talk is about 55 words. Holds, pauses and chimes take their own seconds. Write the skeleton first (the `movements:` line and the `@@` lines with their counts, holds and `[reps N]` after each counted set's go, and an empty `[story] [/story]` after the go of each steady timed set that will carry a piece, no words yet): its build gives each segment's word budget, the reps' quiet left out, and every segment is written to its budget.
- Counts: write a countdown as `[count 5]` (five down to one) or `[count 3 go]` (then the cue; the cues are go, rest, switch, switch sides, stop and hold), and a cue said alone as `[cue rest]`. Coach Freya has no recorded counts, so the voice says it in words ("Three, two, one, go."), quickly: one per segment.
- Voice: Coach Freya is a web voice that reads a whole paragraph at once, so short cues sound fine.

glute bridge (lying):
    Setup: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat and hip width apart.
    Cues: Ribs down, then lift the hips. Squeeze the glutes at the top and hold one beat. Lower one notch at a time.
    Rep: One rep is lifting your hips until your body makes a straight line from knees to shoulders, then lowering back down.
    Feel: Feel it in the back of the hips and the hamstrings, not the low back.
    Faults: If your low back arches, tuck your ribs down and stop the lift sooner. If you feel it in the hamstrings only, pull your heels a little closer. If your knees drift apart, keep them hip width.
    Harder: single-leg glute bridge, dumbbell glute bridge, hip thrust
  push-up (all-fours):
    Setup: Hands under your shoulders, body in one long line from head to heels, or from head to knees.
    Cues: Push the floor away. Ribs down, glutes tight. Elbows at a gentle angle, not flared.
    Rep: One rep is lowering your chest toward the floor and pressing back up to straight arms.
    Feel: Feel it in the chest, the fronts of the shoulders and the backs of the arms, with your core tight and no sag in the low back.
    Faults: If your hips sag, squeeze the glutes and brace your belly. If your elbows flare wide, tuck them to a gentle angle. If you only go halfway, lower your chest a little closer to the floor.
    Easier: incline push-up
    Harder: weighted vest push-up, handle push-up
  prone y t w raise (lying):
    Setup: Lie face down, forehead resting on a folded towel or your hands, arms long.
    Cues: Lift the arms in a Y, then a T, then a W. Thumbs up, shoulders away from your ears. Small and slow, no weight needed.
    Rep: One rep is a Y, then a T, then a W, lifting and lowering each one. All three together count as one rep.
    Feel: Feel it in the upper back between the shoulder blades, not in the neck or the low back.
    Faults: If your neck strains, keep your forehead resting and look at the floor. If you shrug, slide your shoulders away from your ears. If your low back arches, keep your legs and belly relaxed and lift only the arms.

glute bridge (lying):
    Setup: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat and hip width apart.
    Cues: Ribs down, then lift the hips. Squeeze the glutes at the top and hold one beat. Lower one notch at a time.
    Rep: One rep is lifting your hips until your body makes a straight line from knees to shoulders, then lowering back down.
    Feel: Feel it in the back of the hips and the hamstrings, not the low back.
    Faults: If your low back arches, tuck your ribs down and stop the lift sooner. If you feel it in the hamstrings only, pull your heels a little closer. If your knees drift apart, keep them hip width.
    Harder: single-leg glute bridge, dumbbell glute bridge, hip thrust
  push-up (all-fours):
    Setup: Hands under your shoulders, body in one long line from head to heels, or from head to knees.
    Cues: Push the floor away. Ribs down, glutes tight. Elbows at a gentle angle, not flared.
    Rep: One rep is lowering your chest toward the floor and pressing back up to straight arms.
    Feel: Feel it in the chest, the fronts of the shoulders and the backs of the arms, with your core tight and no sag in the low back.
    Faults: If your hips sag, squeeze the glutes and brace your belly. If your elbows flare wide, tuck them to a gentle angle. If you only go halfway, lower your chest a little closer to the floor.
    Easier: incline push-up
    Harder: weighted vest push-up, handle push-up

    Setup: Lie face down, forehead resting on a folded towel or your hands, arms long.
    Cues: Lift the arms in a Y, then a T, then a W. Thumbs up, shoulders away from your ears. Small and slow, no weight needed.

    Feel: Feel it in the upper back between the shoulder blades, not in the neck or the low back.
    Faults: If your neck strains, keep your forehead resting and look at the floor. If you shrug, slide your shoulders away from your ears. If your low back arches, keep your legs and belly relaxed and lift only the arms.

Tell it: the phrase, what it means, said once more slowly. End on the phrase used again later in the session. Not more than one phrase.
